classification.difficultyReason: Find distinct rectangular arrangements without counting rotations twice, then interpret patterns across the arrangements to formulate conclusions.

questions.mappingNote: The task assesses factor pairs through rectangular arrays and invites conclusions about primes, composites and square numbers.
questions.methodNote: Construct rectangular arrays using counters; arrangements obtained by exchanging rows and columns count as the same.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Systematically find rectangular arrangements for twenty numbers and infer patterns from their factor pairs.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the three factor pairs of 12 using rectangular arrays, then list its factors.

questions.mappingNote: Both requests concern the factor pairs and factors of 12, directly assessing find-factors-of-number.
questions.methodNote: Use rectangular arrays to identify factor pairs. Page 1 explicitly treats exchanged rows and columns as the same arrangement; page 2 connects arrays and exact division to factors.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the three factor pairs of 12 using rectangular arrays, then list its factors.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify listed numbers divisible exactly by three.

questions.mappingNote: Select candidates having three as a factor using multiplication pairs.
questions.methodNote: A factor divides a number exactly, with no remainder.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify listed numbers divisible exactly by three.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify exact multiples of twelve among listed numbers.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed relationship is whether twelve is a factor of each candidate.
questions.methodNote: Use exact division or multiplication pairs to identify factors.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify exact multiples of twelve among listed numbers.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise exact whole-number products of seventeen.

questions.mappingNote: Select the exact products of seventeen from the candidates.
questions.methodNote: Multiples are whole-number products; Example 3 explicitly lists multiples of seventeen.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise exact whole-number products of seventeen.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret having seventy-two as a multiple as being a factor of seventy-two.

questions.mappingNote: The wording reverses the usual multiple question and directly assesses identifying factors of seventy-two.
questions.methodNote: Connect a whole-number product with its factors and multiples; use factor pairs.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interpret having seventy-two as a multiple as being a factor of seventy-two.

classification.difficultyReason: Find factor pairs satisfying the additional condition that both factors exceed ten.

questions.mappingNote: Expressing a number as a product with constrained factors directly matches the factors skill.
questions.methodNote: Use the systematic factor-pair method of Example 2 and retain pairs meeting the stated bound.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find factor pairs satisfying the additional condition that both factors exceed ten.

classification.difficultyReason: Find two complete factor lists and identify every shared entry.

questions.mappingNote: The task asks for all common factors, so the factors skill is closer than finding only the highest common factor.
questions.methodNote: List factors using complete factor pairs, then compare the lists.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find two complete factor lists and identify every shared entry.

classification.difficultyReason: List multiples of two numbers and identify common entries in the finite lists.

questions.mappingNote: The closest supplied skill is common multiples through listing, although this task does not ask only for the lowest positive common multiple.
questions.methodNote: Example 3 starts the first eleven multiples at zero. The common-multiples teaching compares the entries in two lists.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: List multiples of two numbers and identify common entries in the finite lists.

classification.difficultyReason: Find neighbouring multiples of 7 and compare their distances from each target.

questions.mappingNote: Each part assesses products with 7 and numerical comparison. Products-multiplication is the closest supplied catalogue skill; finding an LCM is not required.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 lists multiples of 7 by counting in sevens. Page 3 defines a multiple as a whole-number product, and page 4 Example 3 demonstrates listing multiples. Identify the multiples immediately below and above each target and compare distances.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find neighbouring multiples of 7 and compare their distances from each target.

classification.difficultyReason: Compare neighbouring multiples of 11 to identify the closest exactly divisible number.

questions.mappingNote: Connecting exact division with multiplication is the closest supplied skill: each response identifies a multiple of 11 and compares its distance with the adjacent multiple.
questions.methodNote: Pages 2–3 define multiples as whole-number products and factors as numbers that divide exactly. Example 3 on page 4 lists multiples by repeated counting. Compare the two neighbouring multiples of 11 by their distances from the given number.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare neighbouring multiples of 11 to identify the closest exactly divisible number.

classification.difficultyReason: Find quotients and remainders, identify exact divisions and use paired factors to complete the factor list.

questions.mappingNote: Part a applies quotient/remainder multiplication identities. Part b uses exact division and paired factors to give the complete factor list, making find-factors-of-number the primary assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Local page 2 defines factors through exact division and rectangular arrays; page 3 Example 2 lists factors by pairing products. External Chapter 1 page 25 defines quotient and remainder through dividend = divisor × quotient + remainder, with the remainder less than the divisor. Local page 4 establishes Exercise 2A and its preceding factor-pair practice.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate quotients and remainders for small divisors, then identify all factors using exact division and factor pairs.

classification.difficultyReason: Connect quotients and remainders with exact division, then complete the factor list using factor pairs.

questions.mappingNote: Part a applies multiplication facts to division with remainders. Part b uses exact division and factor pairs to determine every factor of 35, so determining factors is the primary skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 defines factors through exact division. Page 3, Example 2, finds a complete factor list using factor pairs. The external Chapter 1 page defines divisor, quotient and remainder through dividend = divisor × quotient + remainder, with remainder less than divisor.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Connect quotients and remainders with exact division, then complete the factor list using factor pairs.

classification.difficultyReason: Explain general factor and multiple statements using multiplication by one or zero, while respecting the exclusion of zero as a divisor.

questions.mappingNote: Each part assesses factor or multiple relationships rather than a divisibility test. Part b conflicts with the taught prohibition on division by zero when 'every number' includes zero.
questions.methodNote: Use the definition of a factor as an exact divisor and a multiple as a whole-number product. Local pages include zero in lists of multiples. The external division discussion explicitly excludes division by zero.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Explain factor and multiple relationships involving one and zero.

classification.difficultyReason: Find complete factor lists and use their sums to verify the embedded definition of a perfect number, including 496.

questions.mappingNote: Question 16 applies the factor-pairing method to 6, 28 and 496, excludes the number itself, then adds the remaining factors to test its embedded perfect-number definition.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 defines factors through exact division and rectangular arrays. Page 3, Example 2, finds all factors by pairing them. Page 4, Exercise 2A question 2, explicitly practises pairing factors.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find complete factor lists and use their sums to verify the embedded definition of a perfect number, including 496.

classification.difficultyReason: Connect an odd factor count to the single equal-factor pair of a square, then generalise that connection to locate the next and largest eligible squares.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts extend factor pairing to counting distinct factors. The closest catalogue skill is determining factors of a whole number; no index-law or prime-factorisation method is required.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 defines factors through exact division and rectangular arrays. Page 3 Example 2 finds all factors by pairing them; Example 1 includes the equal-factor array for 16. Page 4 Exercise 2A reinforces pairing factors, including 25 and 81.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise how repeated factors in square-number factor pairs produce an odd number of distinct factors, then apply the pattern.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognises and counts odd and even whole numbers within stated bounds.

questions.mappingNote: All parts use parity and bounded counting; part d requires the explicit inclusion of zero.
questions.methodNote: Count in twos using the odd/even lists. Whole numbers include zero.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognises and counts odd and even whole numbers within stated bounds.

classification.difficultyReason: Constructs examples satisfying distinctness, parity and a prescribed total.

questions.mappingNote: Select two distinct even numbers greater than 1 and obtain the odd remainder by subtraction.
questions.methodNote: Use the odd/even definitions and check the sum, consistent with Example 5's numerical checking.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Constructs examples satisfying distinctness, parity and a prescribed total.

classification.difficultyReason: Select the parity of each sum using familiar even-pair and odd-unpaired-unit rules; no explanation is requested.

questions.mappingNote: Combining paired collections explains each addition rule without introducing algebra.
questions.methodNote: Use the two-row arrays and lone-dot description of odd numbers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Completes basic parity rules for addition.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate the supplied products and use their parity to complete the corresponding general multiplication statements.

questions.mappingNote: The first instruction group supplies numerical examples for all three rules in the second group; both remain in one question.
questions.methodNote: Calculate the supplied multiplication facts, then use even pairs and odd lone units to explain product parity.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculates basic products and identifies the corresponding general parity rules.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate the supplied two-reflection cycle into an odd/even rule and apply it to each reflection count.

questions.mappingNote: Divisibility by 2 is the closest supplied catalogue skill: parity determines whether one unpaired reflection remains.
questions.methodNote: Use the odd/even distinction and pairing described on page 6; an even number ends in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8. The question supplies the reflection-pair pattern.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply odd and even number patterns to repeated reflections.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that pairing each soldier with its reflection produces an even total.

questions.mappingNote: Divisibility by 2 is the closest supplied catalogue skill because the assessed conclusion is that a doubled count is even.
questions.methodNote: Page 6 represents even numbers by two equal rows and defines them as multiples of 2. Pair each soldier with its mirror image.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise that pairing each soldier with its reflection produces an even total.

classification.difficultyReason: Follow explicit colouring rules for multiples of 2, 3, 5 and 7, retaining each named prime and the supplied exclusion of one.

questions.mappingNote: The activity directly applies page 8's definition of prime numbers and page 9's printed sieve procedure.
questions.methodNote: Exclude 1, then sieve out composite numbers using multiples of 2, 3, 5 and 7.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Follow a sieve procedure to identify primes across a hundred-square chart.

classification.difficultyReason: List factors and select those that are prime, as demonstrated in Example 6.

questions.mappingNote: Finding factors is the primary task; identifying which listed factors are prime is the additional selection.
questions.methodNote: List all factors, then select primes; page 8 Example 6 explicitly demonstrates this method.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: List factors and select those that are prime, as demonstrated in Example 6.

classification.difficultyReason: Search primes in increasing order for the first pair with a specified difference.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed skill is recognising prime numbers while comparing their differences.
questions.methodNote: Use the ordered prime numbers established by the definition and sieve; test the smallest prime first.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Search primes in increasing order for the first pair with a specified difference.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the completed sieve to select the greatest prime strictly below each stated limit.

questions.mappingNote: Select the greatest number satisfying the source definition of prime.
questions.methodNote: Use the completed sieve to identify primes; scan below the stated bound in descending order.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select the greatest prime below each bound using the sieve or prime definition.

classification.difficultyReason: Select prime numbers whose sum satisfies an odd-number condition.

questions.mappingNote: The task directly assesses selecting prime numbers under a parity condition, so identifying prime and composite numbers is the closest supplied skill.
questions.methodNote: Use the definitions of odd and even numbers and the fact that 2 is the only even prime; check the sum of a selected pair.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select prime numbers whose sum satisfies an odd-number condition.

classification.difficultyReason: Find and check prime pairs systematically for sixteen consecutive even numbers.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed skill is recognising prime numbers while constructing sums. Page 8 defines primes; page 9 supplies the sieve method; page 6 establishes even numbers.
questions.methodNote: Use the definition of a prime number and the primes identified by the sieve below 100 to find two prime addends for each even number.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find and check prime pairs systematically for sixteen consecutive even numbers.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine prime identification with odd-even reasoning and check smaller candidates to establish the smallest answer.

questions.mappingNote: The question directly assesses prime identification within sums; prime-composite-numbers is the closest supplied skill.
questions.methodNote: Use odd-even properties and the fact that 2 is the only even prime. Test odd candidates in increasing order using the prime numbers established by the sieve.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine prime identification with odd-even reasoning and check smaller candidates to establish the smallest answer.

classification.difficultyReason: List successive positive powers of two and evaluate by repeated doubling, with the final value supplied.

questions.mappingNote: The complete instruction parallels Example 7, changing the base to 2 and the final exponent to 10. The printed endpoint value is a permanent given.
questions.methodNote: Example 7 lists successive positive integer powers, expands each as repeated multiplication and evaluates. Pages 10–11 introduce this notation with powers of 3.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Directly applies Example 7 to successive positive integer powers of 2.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the demonstrated power notation and repeatedly multiply by three through exponent five.

questions.mappingNote: Directly assesses successive powers of 3 from exponent 1 through exponent 5.
questions.methodNote: Expand each power into repeated factors and evaluate, following the powers-of-3 demonstrations and Example 7.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluates five successive powers using the repeated-multiplication method demonstrated in the teaching.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the demonstrated power notation and repeatedly multiply by five through exponent five.

questions.mappingNote: The base changes to 5 and the requested sequence ends at exponent 5; no index-law simplification is required.
questions.methodNote: List positive integer powers, expand each into repeated multiplication and evaluate, as in Example 7.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Applies the demonstrated expansion and evaluation method to five successive powers of 5.

classification.difficultyReason: Count repeated equal factors and express each group using an index.

questions.mappingNote: Page 10 defines index notation through repeated multiplication; page 11 expands powers of 3 and explains multiplication of powers; page 12 Example 7 connects repeated factors with powers of 4. Parts a and b reverse that expansion directly; parts c and d apply it independently to each group of equal factors.
questions.methodNote: Count equal factors; the repeated factor is the base and its count is the index. Keep different bases as separate powers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Count repeated equal factors and express each group using an index.

classification.difficultyReason: Find missing indices by applying the multiplication law in reverse, including implicit indices of one.

questions.mappingNote: Page 10 establishes index notation and first powers; page 11 states and demonstrates the multiplication rule. Page 12 Example 8 demonstrates completion of a missing index and explicitly counts an unmarked factor as a first power. All six parts apply this same rule in reverse.
questions.methodNote: Use the rule that multiplying powers with the same base adds their indices. A base written without an index has index one. Subtract the supplied indices from the result's index to find the missing index.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find missing indices by applying the multiplication law in reverse, including implicit indices of one.

classification.difficultyReason: Group repeated numerical factors and combine powers with the same base, including implicit indices of one.

questions.mappingNote: Part a counts repeated factors. Parts b and f combine explicit powers with single factors. Part c combines repeated single factors and existing powers for each base. Parts d and e first collect equal factors, then express each repeated group as a power. These are numerical applications of the taught multiplication rule.
questions.methodNote: Index notation records repeated factors. When multiplying powers of the same base, add their indices; a single factor has index one. Page 11 states and demonstrates the rule; page 12 Examples 8 and 9 show adding indices explicitly before simplifying.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Group repeated numerical factors and combine powers with the same base, including implicit indices of one.

classification.difficultyReason: Distinguishes powers of products from multiplication by powers and evaluates products involving powers of ten.

questions.mappingNote: Page 10 defines powers. Page 11 contrasts multiplication by a power with a power of a bracketed product and teaches multiplication of powers with a common base. Page 12 Examples 7–9 reinforce power evaluation and addition of indices. These methods directly support a–f and g–h respectively.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate brackets first, then powers, then multiplication. For products of powers with the same base, add the indices.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Distinguishes powers of products from multiplication by powers and evaluates products involving powers of ten.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine powers of ten and interpret the resulting products to count zeros.

questions.mappingNote: Page 11 demonstrates multiplication of powers of ten by adding indices. Page 12 Examples 8 and 9 reinforce this rule. Part a applies it directly; part b additionally groups and multiplies the numerical factors before counting zeros.
questions.methodNote: Add indices when multiplying powers with the same base; multiply numerical factors separately and interpret powers of ten using place value.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine powers of ten and interpret the resulting products to count zeros.

classification.difficultyReason: Reverse the index-addition rule to express the twentieth power as two tenth powers, substitute 1024 and perform the requested long multiplication.

questions.mappingNote: Pages 10–12 explain powers and adding indices when multiplying powers with the same base. Chapter 1 page 22 demonstrates column partial products for two- and three-digit multipliers; the same place-value method extends to 1024. The prompt supplies the preceding question's result, so this task is self-contained.
questions.methodNote: Use the same-base multiplication rule to express the twentieth power as the product of two tenth powers. Substitute the supplied value, then use vertically aligned partial products with place-value zeros, as taught in the original Chapter 1 multiplication examples.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise two equal powers as factors, then extend the taught column multiplication method to a four-digit multiplier.

classification.difficultyReason: Select and show efficient mental multiplication steps using factorisation, doubling and halving.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts ask for mental multiplication working. Factor regrouping is used in a, b, d and e; doubling and halving is used in c, f, g and h. These preserve the source-taught methods without using a written multiplication algorithm.
questions.methodNote: Page 14 groups factors to simplify products and demonstrates repeated doubling. Page 15 teaches doubling one factor while halving the other and demonstrates these methods in Example 10. Page 16 confirms the Exercise 2E boundary.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select and show efficient mental multiplication steps using factorisation, doubling and halving.

classification.difficultyReason: Select and show suitable mental strategies for multiplication and division with larger numbers.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and f use the doubling-and-halving method on page 15. Part b combines that method with multiplication by 11 on pages 15–16. Part c follows Example 12(b), simplifying division by 50 to division by 5. Part d follows repeated halving in Example 12(a). Part e follows Example 11(b). The mixed selection directly assesses choosing efficient mental strategies.
questions.methodNote: Use doubling and halving, multiplication by 11 as ten times plus the original number, multiplication by 9 as ten times minus the original number, division by 5 through doubling and dividing by 10, and repeated halving for division by 16.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select and show suitable mental strategies for multiplication and division with larger numbers.

classification.difficultyReason: Systematically test prime divisors, including finding 29 as a factor of 841, then express repeated primes using powers; no new method is needed.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly requests prime factorisation. The worked answers use repeated factorisation and collect repeated primes, consistent with the inspected teaching. Question 2 is a separate complete task from Question 1.
questions.methodNote: Pages 2–3 establish factors and factor pairs. Page 17 expresses prime factorisations with primes in increasing order. Page 18 teaches repeated factorisation, repeated division and factor trees; Example 13 on page 19 collects repeated prime factors in index notation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the taught prime-factorisation methods to six whole numbers, collecting repeated prime factors in index notation.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate three given powers, then multiply their values.

questions.mappingNote: Each part reverses a supplied prime factorisation by evaluating its powers and multiplying. Order of operations with indices is the most advanced directly assessed catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Pages 10–11 explain powers as repeated multiplication and explicitly require evaluating indices before multiplication. Pages 17–19 connect products of prime powers with their whole-number values.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate three given powers, then multiply their values.

classification.difficultyReason: Use two prime factorisations to identify the greatest shared factor.

questions.mappingNote: Part a uses the taught repeated-factorisation method until every factor is prime. Part b compares those prime factors to find the largest common factor, making HCF the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Pages 2–3 define factors as exact divisors. Pages 17–18 teach prime factorisation by repeated factorisation, repeated division and factor trees; Example 13 on page 19 applies repeated division and a factor tree.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use two prime factorisations to identify the greatest shared factor.

classification.difficultyReason: Systematically generate distinct-prime products and justify that every two-digit possibility has been found.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed task is constructing numbers from complete prime factorisations and systematically finding all possibilities; prime-factorisation is the closest catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Pages 17–19 express whole numbers as products of prime factors, arrange primes in increasing order, and demonstrate repeated factorisation, repeated division and factor trees. This task reverses that process by multiplying three distinct primes.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Systematically generate distinct-prime products and justify that every two-digit possibility has been found.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret each square as multiplication of the given integer by itself and calculate directly.

questions.mappingNote: Every part evaluates an integer raised to the power 2; evaluation of index notation is the directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: A square is the number multiplied by itself, as defined on page 20 and reiterated in the page 21 summary.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct evaluation of six whole-number squares using multiplication.

classification.difficultyReason: Connect squaring with the familiar parity rules for multiplication.

questions.mappingNote: The task applies the definition of squaring and multiplication parity. Evaluate numbers in index notation is the closest supplied skill; prime factorisation and root-finding are not assessed.
questions.methodNote: Page 20 defines a square as a number multiplied by itself; page 21 repeats this definition. Exercise 2B question 6 on page 7 establishes that even × even is even and odd × odd is odd, using the parity definitions on page 6.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Connect squaring with the familiar parity rules for multiplication.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the supplied odd parity of both square numbers and apply the rule that odd plus odd is even.

questions.mappingNote: The task applies parity reasoning to square numbers. Evaluating index notation is the closest supplied catalogue skill; no square-root calculation or prime factorisation is required.
